subject: Immunology
vignette: A 28-year-old man returns from a 3-week trip to South Asia with 10 days of stepwise fever, headache, and abdominal discomfort. He then develops sudden severe right lower quadrant pain with guarding. Computed tomography shows free intraperitoneal air and marked thickening of the terminal ileum, and blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod.
question: The bowel lesion responsible for his perforation is located at which of the following sites?

options.text: The Peyer patches of the terminal ileum

explanation_correct: Salmonella typhi enters through the gut by binding to M cells in the dome epithelium overlying Peyer patches, then spreads to mesenteric nodes and the bloodstream, causing the stepwise fever and bacteremia of typhoid. In the third week, the hypertrophied Peyer patches in the terminal ileum undergo necrosis and ulceration along their long axis, which can perforate and produce peritonitis. The terminal ileum, the site of greatest Peyer patch density, is therefore the classic site of typhoid perforation.

explanation_incorrect.A: The gastric fundus is not a site of Peyer patch concentration and is not the classic site of typhoid ulceration.
explanation_incorrect.B: The duodenal bulb lacks organized Peyer patches; duodenal ulcers are typically due to acid-peptic disease or NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.C: Jejunal villi contain few organized lymphoid aggregates, and typhoid lesions are concentrated in the ileum.
explanation_incorrect.D: Colonic haustra do not contain the dense Peyer patch tissue that is the portal of entry for Salmonella typhi.

educationalObjective: Salmonella typhi invades via M cells overlying Peyer patches and classically perforates the terminal ileum in the third week of infection.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has had seven episodes of streptococcal pharyngitis in 2 years and now reports snoring, mouth breathing, and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows enlarged, erythematous palatine tonsils meeting in the midline. He undergoes tonsillectomy with an uncomplicated recovery.
question: Which feature of the palatine tonsils best explains their predilection for recurrent infection and peritonsillar abscess?

options.text: Deep crypts that trap debris and the absence of afferent lymphatic vessels
An extensive network of afferent lymphatic vessels that recirculate bacteria
A fibrous capsule that isolates the organ from systemic immunity
Absence of germinal centers, which prevents local antibody production
A lining of M cells that transports bacteria directly into the bloodstream

explanation_correct: Palatine tonsils are secondary lymphoid organs of Waldeyer ring with deep epithelial crypts that greatly increase surface area for antigen sampling but also trap food debris and bacteria. They lack afferent lymphatic vessels, so material trapped in the crypts is not cleared by lymph flow and can seed recurrent infection or a peritonsillar abscess. Because tonsils are secondary organs, removing them does not meaningfully impair immunity, since mucosal defense is shared with the adenoids, lingual tonsils, and Peyer patches.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tonsils characteristically lack afferent lymphatics; recirculating bacteria through afferent vessels is not their anatomy.
explanation_incorrect.C: The tonsils are not truly encapsulated, and their problem is trapping of organisms in crypts rather than isolation by a capsule.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tonsils contain prominent germinal centers, especially when chronically infected, so they do produce local antibody responses.
explanation_incorrect.E: M cells sample antigen and deliver it to underlying lymphoid tissue; they do not transport organisms directly into the blood.

educationalObjective: Tonsillar crypts trap organisms while the absence of afferent lymphatics predisposes to recurrent infection and peritonsillar abscess.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 57-year-old woman presents with 4 months of epigastric pain and early satiety. Endoscopy shows a superficial gastric ulcer, and biopsy shows a dense infiltrate of small marginal-zone B cells surrounding and invading gastric glands, forming lymphoepithelial lesions. Helicobacter pylori testing is positive. Staging shows disease limited to the stomach, and eradication therapy alone produces regression of the tumor.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this tumor?

options.text: Integrated Epstein-Barr virus genome driving B cell proliferation
t(11;14) translocation causing cyclin D1 overexpression
Chronic antigen-driven proliferation of mucosal marginal-zone B cells
Inactivation of the APC tumor suppressor gene
Defective DNA mismatch repair with microsatellite instability

explanation_correct: Gastric MALT lymphoma arises from mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue that develops in the stomach in response to chronic Helicobacter pylori infection. Continuous T cell-dependent antigenic stimulation drives polyclonal marginal-zone B cell expansion, which can eventually acquire genetic abnormalities; at an early stage the tumor remains antigen dependent and regresses when the organism is eradicated. This is why H. pylori eradication is first-line therapy for localized gastric MALT lymphoma and why the tumor may later develop t(11;18) and become antigen independent.

explanation_incorrect.A: EBV is linked to Burkitt lymphoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, and Hodgkin lymphoma, not typically to gastric MALT lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression is the hallmark of mantle cell lymphoma, which is not antigen driven in this way.
explanation_incorrect.D: APC inactivation underlies familial adenomatous polyposis and colorectal adenocarcinoma, not gastric MALT lymphoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mismatch repair deficiency causes Lynch syndrome-associated colorectal and endometrial cancers, not this H. pylori-driven tumor.

educationalObjective: Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic H. pylori antigenic stimulation of marginal-zone B cells and often regresses with eradication therapy.
